short_definition: Parkinson's Law is the observation that work expands to fill the time available for its completion, so tasks given generous deadlines tend to take longer than they need to.
explanation: Parkinson's Law comes from British historian C. Northcote Parkinson, who described it in a 1955 essay in The Economist about the growth of bureaucracy. In everyday productivity it describes a familiar pattern: give yourself a week for a two-hour task, and the task fills up with extra research, tweaking and procrastination.

Parkinson's Law matters because you can turn it to your advantage. Shorter but realistic deadlines, time-boxing and self-imposed limits (such as finishing a draft before lunch) often get work done faster without much loss of quality. A similar pattern applies to money, where spending tends to rise to match income. That is one reason automating savings before you can spend the money helps.

Parkinson's Law can backfire if you set deadlines that are too tight, leading to rushed work, mistakes and stress. It is an observation, not a scientific law. Use it as a prompt to question how much time a task really needs, not as a reason to squeeze every task.
example: Illustrative example: you set aside a whole Saturday to 'sort out my finances' and spend eight hours bouncing between browser tabs. The next month you time-box the same three tasks (reviewing statements, updating your budget and moving money to savings) into a 90-minute block with a timer, and you finish within that window.
common_mistake: Setting deadlines so tight that quality suffers, or time-boxing work whose real length is genuinely uncertain. The aim is to remove padding, not to rush everything.
title: Parkinson's Law
